docs.title: PlanExe2
docs.text:
PlanExe2 turns a planning idea into a strategic plan draft: a single HTML report that leads with the decisions you still have to make, backed by the supporting analysis and an audit trail of what was checked.

PlanExe v1: generate an unusually comprehensive expert planning workshop.

PlanExe2: construct a partially validated model of the project, then expose what humans still have to decide.

PlanExe2 is PlanExe v1's plan-generation pipeline, rewritten as skills executed by a small, dependency-free Python DAG runner.

  • No pip install. Python 3.11 or newer, standard library only.
  • LLM calls go through the headless Claude Code CLI (claude -p), on your Claude subscription.
  • You don't write the prompt yourself: your coding agent interviews you, drafts the prompt, checks it and launches only after you confirm.
  • Every stage writes plain JSON and markdown files. Edit any of them and re-run: your edit is kept and everything downstream is regenerated.

The output is a draft to refine, not ground truth. It surfaces the questions and decisions a plan depends on.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
• Getting started: requirements and how to make your first plan.
  • The report: what the report contains and how to read it.

docs.title: PlanExe v1
docs.text:
The v1 documentation (MCP server, web frontends, Docker, OpenRouter/Ollama/LM Studio providers) is in the PlanExe repository. PlanExe2 does not have these components.

Source: github.com/PlanExeOrg/PlanExe2.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: The recommended way is to let your coding agent run these. This page is for running PlanExe2 by hand, and for reference. All commands run from the repo root.

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
python3 -m planexe_skill check-prompt --prompt-file my_prompt.txt
python3 -m planexe_skill create runs/my_plan --prompt-file my_prompt.txt
python3 -m planexe_skill run runs/20261008_my_plan

The prompt is flowing prose, typically 300-800 words, not bullet lists or headings. Cover the objective, scope, location, budget, timeline, scale, stakeholders, constraints and success criteria. Label guesses as assumptions. check-prompt (one LLM call) rates each of these as present, partial or missing, suggests questions, and exits with 0 when the prompt is ready.

create names the run directory after the date it is created: runs/my_plan becomes runs/20261008_my_plan, and the path is printed. A name that already starts with yyyymmdd_ is kept; --no-date-prefix uses the path as given. --start-date YYYY-MM-DD sets the plan's Month 0 (default today; past and future dates are fine).

run runs every stage that needs running and resumes where it left off.

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text:
command what it does check-prompt --prompt-file F pre-flight check of a prompt (1 LLM call): usability, completeness, questions create RUN_DIR --prompt-file F [--start-date D] create a run dir (plan_raw.json, start_time.json); D = Month 0 run RUN_DIR run every dirty stage; resumes where it left off run RUN_DIR --only STAGE run one stage (its inputs must already exist) run RUN_DIR --until STAGE run a stage and everything it depends on run RUN_DIR --force STAGE re-run a stage even if it is clean run RUN_DIR --force-downstream STAGE regenerate a stage and everything after it run RUN_DIR --dry-run list stages that would run status RUN_DIR which stages are dirty and why explain RUN_DIR STAGE details for one stage graph [--dot] stages in topological order

create and run also accept --prompt TEXT instead of a file, and --plan-raw FILE to copy an existing plan_raw.json (keeping its date).

docs.title: Options for run
docs.text:
option default --workers N 4 concurrent LLM calls --model-high M claude-sonnet-5-5 model for tier: high stages --model-mid M claude-sonnet-5-5 model for tier: mid stages --model-low M claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 model for tier: low stages --backend B claude claude (Claude Code CLI) or opencode (opencode CLI) --model M model for every tier; the --model-TIER options override it

check-prompt also accepts --backend and --model.

docs.title: Running on other models with opencode
docs.text:
--backend opencode makes every LLM call through the headless opencode CLI (opencode run), so a plan can be generated by any model opencode can reach. Configure a provider first (opencode auth login), pick a model from opencode models, and give it as PROVIDER/MODEL:

python3 -m planexe_skill run runs/<yyyymmdd>_<name> --backend opencode --model openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k2.6

There is no default model for this backend. Give --model for all tiers, or --model-high/--model-mid/ --model-low to mix models (an unset tier falls back to the mid model, then the high one).

  • Each call runs with opencode's project config, plugins, CLAUDE.md files and tools switched off, and the stage's system prompt as the agent prompt. tier: high stages may use opencode's websearch tool.
  • opencode has no schema-enforced output: the model replies with JSON, which is validated against the schema, and the problems are sent back on a retry. Weaker models need more retries, or fail a stage.
  • opencode's own free models (opencode/..., e.g. opencode/glm-5.3-flash-free) work too. Their free tier refuses requests that carry no tools, so for these models the read tool stays listed (with every permission denied, so it can't actually run).
  • Sessions go to a private database in the temp dir, not to your opencode session history.

docs.title: Progress, logs and stopping
docs.text:
• Progress is printed with an ETA and mirrored to RUN_DIR/.planexe_skill/progress.json.
  • Per-stage logs, with every prompt and response, are in RUN_DIR/.planexe_skill/logs/.
  • To stop gracefully, create the file RUN_DIR/.planexe_skill/stop.

docs.title: Failures and resuming
docs.text:
LLM calls stream their output. A call that produces nothing for 90 seconds is killed and retried once, and no call may run longer than 10 minutes. Completed LLM calls inside a stage are cached, so re-running after a failure only repeats the calls that didn't finish.

On failure the runner prints the failing stage, the error, the log path and a retry command. To resume, run python3 -m planexe_skill run RUN_DIR again.

The child claude process needs keychain access, so run outside any sandbox. If authentication fails, run claude auth login and resume.

docs.title: Versioning and report metadata
docs.text:
Every report's Metadata section names its generator version (git describe: v2.0.0 on the tag, v2.0.0-3-gabc1234 three commits later, +modified for uncommitted changes), repo and commit.

A run can mix code versions (resumed runs, stages regenerated after an edit), so this is recorded per stage in RUN_DIR/planexe_report_metadata.json: generator version and commit, when it ran, which models it used, how many LLM calls and web searches it made, plus hand-edited intermediary files and adopted stages. Each *_raw.json also carries metadata.generator (repo, commit, git tag).

The plan's start date (Month 0, start_time.json) is independent of when the plan is generated, so plans can be dated in the past or the future.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or newer. Standard library only; nothing to pip install.
  • The Claude Code CLI, logged in: claude auth login. PlanExe2 makes its LLM calls through it, on your Claude subscription.
  • Usage budget: a full plan is about 220-260 LLM calls and takes roughly 65-90 minutes.

docs.title: Recommended: clone the repo and ask your coding agent
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/PlanExeOrg/PlanExe2.git
cd PlanExe2
claude

Then ask for a plan, for example "make a plan for a bakery in Lyon". Codex and other agents follow the same steps via AGENTS.md.

docs.title: What the agent does
docs.text:
The make-plan skill (.claude/skills/make-plan/) takes over:

  1. Asks a few questions about what the plan needs and you haven't said yet: objective, location, budget, timeline, scale, stakeholders, constraints, success criteria. Each question comes with suggested answers to pick from, and "you decide" where a sensible default exists. It also asks for the plan's start date (Month 0); past and future dates are fine.
  2. Drafts the prompt: 300-800 words of prose built from your answers. Anything it assumed on your behalf is labelled as an assumption, so the plan treats it as an estimate.
  3. Checks the prompt with check-prompt (one LLM call). If important items are missing, it asks again.
  4. Asks for confirmation. It shows the prompt, the check result, the start date and the cost, and launches only after you say yes.
  5. Runs the plan in the background and reports back when it is done, starting with the decisions you need to make.

docs.title: While it runs
docs.text: Progress lines show the current stage and an ETA based on the DAG's critical path. The same data is in runs/<yyyymmdd>_<name>/.planexe_skill/progress.json. If something fails, re-running resumes where it stopped; finished stages and completed LLM calls are kept.

docs.title: The result
docs.text:
Plans are written to runs/<yyyymmdd>_<name>/ inside the clone (ignored by git), for example runs/20261008_cross_border_rail_ticketing/. Open report.html; report.md has the same content. See The report for what is in it.

Update with git pull. Each report's Metadata section names the PlanExe2 version that produced it.

docs.title: Without git: let the agent fetch it
docs.text:
In any Claude Code session, paste:

Clone https://github.com/PlanExeOrg/PlanExe2, read its CLAUDE.md, and use its make-plan skill to make me a plan for a bakery in Lyon.

This works, but a session started outside the repo does not load the repo's skill on its own, so the agent has to find and read CLAUDE.md first. Cloning and starting the agent inside the repo is more reliable.

docs.title: Sandboxed agents
docs.text: The child claude process needs keychain access for authentication. If your agent runs commands in a sandbox (for example Claude Code desktop with sandbox on), the plan run must happen outside it. If authentication fails, run claude auth login and resume.

docs.title: Why there is no pip package
docs.text: There are no dependencies to install, and the skills, prompts and schemas live in the repo next to the agent instructions that drive them. A pip package would move the make-plan skill out of your project and need a separate install step for the guided flow. A Claude Code plugin is the likely route if PlanExe2 should work from any folder without cloning.

docs.text:

  • Understand what gets generated and why: How it works.

docs.title: A DAG of skills
docs.text:
Plan generation is a pipeline of about 75 stages. Each stage is a skill: a folder in skills/ with its prompts, an output schema and a small run.py. A dependency-free Python runner (planexe_skill/) executes them as a DAG, with up to 4 LLM calls in parallel by default.

Edges are derived from file names: a stage depends on whichever stage produces one of its inputs. Run python3 -m planexe_skill graph to list the stages in order, or graph --dot for Graphviz.

docs.title: A skill folder
docs.text:
skills/identify_purpose/
  SKILL.md        frontmatter (inputs, outputs, tier, est_llm_calls) + description
  prompts/        system prompts, verbatim from PlanExe v1 unless noted
  schema.json     JSON schema for structured output
  run.py          def run(ctx): reads inputs, calls ctx.llm(...), writes outputs

A skill may only read the files listed in its inputs and write the files listed in its outputs; the runner enforces this.

docs.title: Tiers
docs.text:
Each skill's tier picks the model:

tier default model used for high Sonnet, high effort the foundational early stages mid Sonnet, low effort later stages where the fast model isn't good enough low Haiku, no extended thinking everything else

Override with --model-high, --model-mid and --model-low (see Commands).

docs.title: Intermediary files
docs.text: Every stage writes plain JSON and markdown files, all in the run directory. The report is assembled from them at the end.

docs.title: Dirtiness
docs.text:
RUN_DIR/.planexe_skill/manifest.json stores, for every stage, hashes of its skill folder, its input files and its output files. A stage is dirty, and re-runs, when:

  • one of its outputs is missing,
  • its skill folder changed, or
  • one of its inputs changed.

python3 -m planexe_skill status RUN_DIR shows which stages are dirty and why.

docs.title: Editing and re-running
docs.text:
You can edit any intermediary file by hand, for example to correct a budget in an early stage or rewrite an assumption. On the next run:

  • your edited file is kept (the stage that produced it is not re-run over your edit),
  • every stage downstream of it is dirty and is regenerated from your version.

Hand-edited files are listed in the report's Metadata section.

To regenerate a stage instead of editing it, use run RUN_DIR --force STAGE, or --force-downstream STAGE to also regenerate everything after it.

docs.title: Stages added by PlanExe2
docs.text:
These stages are not in PlanExe v1:

stage what it does canonical_facts one table of key numbers and dates, produced before the project plan consistency_review lints the core documents against the canonical facts consistency_repair repairs them with exact edits, including deterministic arithmetic fixes decision_register the open decisions as options, consequences, owner and deadline, plus the choices to ratify arithmetic_check deterministic re-computation of every written calculation

docs.title: The report
docs.text: A finished run produces report.html (and the same content as report.md) in its run directory. The report leads with the decisions and key facts, not the workshop. It has three parts.

docs.title: Part 1: Key decisions and facts
docs.text:
Start here. These sections are what a human has to act on.

section what it is for Decision Dashboard The go/no-go gates the plan depends on. Decisions Required Each open decision with its options, downstream consequences, an owner and a decide-by month, ranked by importance. Ends with Choices made on your behalf: strategic choices the generator made to complete the plan, for you to ratify or reject. Canonical Facts One table of the key numbers and dates. Every other section is checked against it. Executive Summary Scope, goals, deliverables, timeline, budget and main risks. If this is wrong, the rest will be wrong too. Gantt A draft schedule computed from the estimated durations and dependencies.

docs.title: Part 2: Supporting analysis
docs.text:
PlanExe's planning documents. Use them to understand and challenge the decisions in Part 1.

  • Pitch and Project Plan (SMART criteria, dependencies, resources, stakeholders, regulatory requirements).
  • Strategic Decisions and Scenarios: the levers the plan considered and the path it chose.
  • Assumptions, Physical Locations, Currency Strategy, Risks.
  • Governance: bodies, implementation plan, escalation matrix, progress monitoring.
  • Data Collection, Documents to Create and Find.
  • SWOT Analysis, Team.
  • Expert Criticism: the plan reviewed from several specialist viewpoints.
  • Work Breakdown Structure, Review Plan, Questions & Answers.
  • Premortem and Self Audit: adversarial sections that assume the plan failed and look for why.

docs.title: Part 3: Audit trail
docs.text:
What was checked, and what was not.

section what it tells you Validation Status What "validated" means for this report: which sections searched the web, the consistency lint result before and after repair, a deterministic re-computation of every written calculation, and which sections were not checked. Consistency Check The full lint of the core documents against the Canonical Facts. If the lint still fails after repair, the report shows a "Consistency lint FAILED" banner. Initial Prompt Vetted How the prompt was screened before planning. Prompt Adherence Whether the plan kept to what the prompt asked for. Metadata Generator version and commit, and per stage: when it ran, which models it used, LLM calls and web searches, and which files were hand-edited.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Go through Decisions Required and Choices made on your behalf. Correct anything that doesn't match your situation.
  2. Check the Canonical Facts and Executive Summary for scope, budget and timeline.
  3. Read Validation Status to see which parts are unchecked.
  4. Use Part 2 to challenge the plan with stakeholders and domain experts.

To change something, edit the relevant intermediary file in the run directory and re-run; see How it works.

docs.title: When Planning Becomes Cheap: The Future of Work in an Age of AI
docs.text:
This essay is a speculative assessment written by GPT-6, an AI model; "I" in the text is the AI author. The predictions are not established facts, and the opinions should not be treated as independent research findings. The cited studies provide context for the discussion; they do not validate the predictions or establish the effectiveness of PlanExe.

What happens when AI can explore hundreds of ideas, develop detailed plans, and perform work that once required teams of professionals?

docs.title: 1. A different kind of automation
docs.text:
For decades, computers have helped people work faster. Spreadsheets made calculations easier, search engines made information easier to find, and software automated repetitive tasks.

Artificial intelligence is beginning to automate something different: the work involved in investigating problems and deciding what might be done about them.

AI can already help research a subject, develop alternative strategies, estimate costs, identify risks, and produce detailed project plans. Some systems can perform many of these steps without a person guiding each one.

This does not mean the results are always correct. AI can misunderstand requirements, invent facts, make calculation errors, and confidently recommend bad ideas.

But something important has changed.

Producing a detailed plan is becoming much cheaper. Establishing whether that plan is worth trusting is not.

I think this distinction will shape the future of work more than the ability to generate impressive documents.

docs.title: From assistant to autonomous planner
docs.text:
Most people know AI as something they ask questions.

They ask for a business plan, a comparison of products, or help with a difficult decision. The AI answers, and the person decides what to ask next.

Autonomous planning systems take this further.

A person describes a goal. The system then explores possible approaches, examines risks, develops schedules and budgets, challenges assumptions, and organizes the results into a plan.

One example is PlanExe, an open-source system designed to turn a project description into a comprehensive planning report.

PlanExe uses several stages of AI analysis, including different strategic approaches, failure analysis, decision points, and consistency checks. It also attempts to distinguish user requirements from assumptions and estimates.

That does not make its conclusions independently verified or guarantee that it produces good plans. But it illustrates a wider shift: more of the planning process can happen without a human managing every intermediate step.

The consequence could be significant. Planning may become less about producing one answer and more about exploring many possible answers.

docs.title: 2. From three ideas to one hundred
docs.text:
Imagine a company considering how to manufacture a new product.

Traditionally, it might pay consultants to investigate three approaches. The work is expensive, so it has to choose which ideas deserve investigation before much evidence is available.

Now imagine AI makes it affordable to generate a hundred preliminary plans.

The company could compare ten manufacturing approaches with ten different business models.

That gives it one hundred combinations to investigate.

This technique is sometimes called grid search. The idea is simple: systematically try different combinations instead of relying on a few educated guesses.

If generating one plan cost $0.50 in AI model fees, generating one hundred would cost $50. That is an illustration, not a fixed price for PlanExe or any other tool. Actual costs vary by model, workload, provider, and infrastructure.

More importantly, the generation cost excludes the work of checking the plans.

docs.title: The problem moves from generating to choosing
docs.text:
Suppose an AI system produces one hundred convincing plans.

Which one should the company choose?

Asking the same AI to give each plan a score from 1 to 10 is tempting, but potentially dangerous.

It might prefer plans that sound impressive rather than plans that can succeed. It might reward detailed budgets even when their underlying assumptions are wrong.

This is related to Goodhart's law: when people or systems optimize for a particular measurement, that measurement can become less useful as an indicator of genuine success.

For example, if an AI is rewarded for producing plans with low costs, it may consistently choose optimistic cost assumptions. The plans score well, but they are not necessarily affordable.

A better approach would use several stages.

First, eliminate plans that violate requirements such as a hard budget limit or safety constraint. Check arithmetic using conventional software where possible.

Next, compare the surviving plans using the same assumptions and clearly defined criteria. Look for unsupported claims, uncertainty, and major differences between their approaches.

Then have independent reviewers examine a small number of promising candidates. Where possible, use experiments, supplier quotations, customer evidence, or real-world tests to settle disagreements.

Not every project needs one overall winner. Sometimes the useful result is a shortlist: one option is inexpensive, another is safer, and a third performs better under difficult conditions.

Even then, the work can be substantial. If ten shortlisted plans each require two hours of review, and three finalists each need eight additional hours of specialist examination, that is 44 hours of human work.

The AI generation may cost very little, but human attention becomes the scarce resource.

And if the original data is unreliable, producing more plans will not fix it.

docs.title: Could cheaper planning actually make decisions worse?
docs.text:
Yes.

An organization might become overwhelmed by alternatives. Managers could repeatedly reconsider projects because a newly generated plan looks more attractive.

People might also confuse having explored many possibilities with having gathered more evidence.

One hundred plans based on the same untested assumption are not one hundred independent confirmations.

The goal should not be to produce as many plans as possible. It should be to discover better options, reject weak ones early, and make better decisions.

docs.title: 3. How work will change
docs.text:
I expect AI to affect professions centered on information, analysis, documentation, and recommendations.

This includes consulting, administration, software development, financial analysis, research, policy work, and project planning.

The change will not be uniform.

A consultant may spend less time producing an initial report and more time checking whether its recommendations are defensible.

A project manager may spend less time preparing schedules and more time resolving disagreements, negotiating commitments, and dealing with unexpected events.

A researcher may spend less time developing initial hypotheses and more time designing experiments to test them.

The work shifts from creating possible answers toward evaluating which answers deserve confidence.

docs.title: Will jobs disappear?
docs.text:
Some probably will.

Jobs do not need to be fully automated to disappear. If AI removes enough of the work that supports a position, an organization may decide it needs fewer employees.

Consider a team of five analysts primarily producing planning documents. If two people equipped with AI can produce the same amount of acceptable work, the organization may reduce the team.

But another organization might retain all five and investigate many more opportunities.

Economists have long studied a related effect, sometimes associated with Jevons' paradox: making something cheaper can increase demand for it. The effect does not necessarily apply to every service, but it is relevant here.

Cheaper planning could result in fewer planning jobs, more planning work, or both.

The evidence so far suggests caution about sweeping claims.

A 2025 International Labour Organization study estimated that one in four workers worldwide were in occupations with some exposure to generative AI. It concluded that changes to jobs were more likely than their complete elimination.

A 2026 ILO review found uneven productivity gains and limited evidence of widespread displacement at that point.

So the claim that AI will replace large parts of the workforce is not yet supported by observed employment data. But neither is the claim that most jobs are safe.

docs.title: Who trains the next generation?
docs.text:
One particularly difficult problem involves people entering the workforce.

Junior employees often learn by doing simpler tasks.

New analysts prepare reports. Young developers fix bugs. Researchers review existing work. Junior consultants investigate limited parts of larger projects.

These activities teach people how to recognize problems, understand consequences, and develop judgment.

If AI takes over much of that work, how do juniors become seniors?

This is not merely hypothetical. An August 2026 Stanford study found that employment among workers aged 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations was approximately 19% below where it would have been if it had followed the growth of less-exposed peers. The researchers emphasized that this was not proof AI caused the difference.

Organizations may need to redesign junior roles around supervised evaluation, real-world experience, and learning how to challenge AI-generated work.

Otherwise, they risk removing the training opportunities that produce their future experts.

docs.title: Who receives the savings?
docs.text:
Higher productivity does not guarantee higher wages or shorter working hours.

Companies might reduce prices, expand their services, increase profits, reduce staff, or simply demand more work from fewer people.

The outcome depends on business decisions, competition, labor arrangements, and public policy.

One possible future involves smaller teams serving more customers. Another involves more opportunities for individuals and small organizations. A less attractive outcome involves a growing concentration of income among those who own the tools and infrastructure.

AI makes these possibilities more immediate, but it does not determine which one society chooses.

docs.title: 4. The coming problem of trust
docs.text:
As AI makes reports, proposals, and research cheaper, we should expect much more of them.

Some will be valuable. Others will be polished documents containing unsupported claims, unrealistic assumptions, or little original insight.

People increasingly describe low-value AI-generated material as slop.

The difficulty is that useful and useless material can look similar.

Both may contain professional formatting, detailed calculations, and confident recommendations.

A long report is no longer evidence that someone invested substantial time investigating the problem.

docs.title: What would make AI-generated work trustworthy?
docs.text:
I would look for a few basic properties.

The work should distinguish facts from estimates, explain where important claims came from, and identify which assumptions have not been tested.

It should make contradictions visible and show which decisions remain unresolved.

Where possible, calculations should be reproducible using ordinary software.

And most importantly, it should not confuse AI checking its own output with independent verification.

A system can run multiple AI reviews and still repeat the same underlying mistake.

This is one reason transparent tools matter. Systems such as PlanExe attempt to show decisions, assumptions, criticism, and unresolved problems rather than presenting only a polished conclusion.

That is a useful design direction, but it is not proof of correctness. The checks themselves must be tested.

docs.title: What if everyone uses similar AI?
docs.text:
There is another risk: many organizations may receive similar recommendations because their AI systems rely on similar models and information.

This is sometimes called algorithmic monoculture.

If thousands of businesses independently ask AI where to invest, they might all identify the same opportunity. If their assumptions share a weakness, the same mistake could spread widely.

Using several AI agents does not guarantee independent judgment.

Different data sources, competing assumptions, independent tests, and human expertise will remain important.

The purpose of criticism is not simply to create disagreement. It is to discover which claims survive being challenged.

docs.title: 5. Where I think we are going
docs.text:
My expectation is that AI will become increasingly capable of producing preliminary professional work, while the difficulty of verifying that work will become more visible.

That is a prediction. It should be judged against evidence, not accepted because it sounds reasonable.

Here are three more specific predictions.

docs.title: Prediction 1: Producing first drafts will become dramatically faster
docs.text:
By the end of 2030, organizations that regularly use autonomous AI systems for planning will need at least 50% fewer human hours to produce comparable first drafts than they needed with their previous manual workflows.

This could be tested by comparing actual projects of similar size, with clearly defined requirements and time records.

It could be wrong. Organizations might discover that preparing inputs, correcting errors, and maintaining the systems consume most of the time saved.

docs.title: Prediction 2: Verification will become a larger share of planning work
docs.text:
By the end of 2030, in organizations successfully using autonomous planning systems, reviewing and validating AI-generated material will account for more human planning time than drafting it.

This would represent a meaningful change in professional work.

It could be tested through workplace studies that measure how employees spend their time.

If professionals still spend most of their effort writing initial plans, this prediction has failed.

docs.title: Prediction 3: More alternatives will not automatically produce better decisions
docs.text:
By the end of 2030, I expect controlled studies to show that generating many more candidate plans does not consistently improve the final decision unless the evaluation process also improves.

Researchers could test this by giving different groups the same problem. One receives a few carefully developed alternatives; another receives many AI-generated alternatives; a third receives many alternatives with independent checking and structured comparison.

The results should be judged by expert evaluation and, where possible, real-world outcomes—not by how convincing the reports look.

It is possible that simply exploring many alternatives will outperform my expectations. That would be an important result too.

docs.title: The questions that remain
docs.text:
Several questions will become more difficult as AI systems improve.

What happens when the number of proposals grows much faster than an organization's ability to make decisions?

How do we train experts if much of their early work is automated?

Who is responsible when an AI-generated recommendation causes harm?

Can small organizations actually benefit from cheap planning if they still lack funding and influence?

What happens when AI systems produce many plausible strategies but cannot establish which one will work?

And perhaps the most consequential question:

If AI allows society to produce much more valuable work with fewer people, how will the benefits be shared?

These are not questions that better language models can answer on their own.

They require choices by people, organizations, and institutions.

docs.title: Conclusion: Cheap to produce, expensive to trust
docs.text:
I expect AI to change professional work substantially, particularly where people are paid to gather information, develop alternatives, and prepare documents.

Some jobs will disappear. Others will change. New opportunities will emerge as more people gain access to powerful planning and research tools.

But the most important change may be in how we judge the value of intellectual work.

A detailed plan may no longer represent weeks of professional effort. It may represent an inexpensive automated process.

That does not make the plan worthless. It means we need better ways to evaluate its quality.

The ability to produce a hundred plans is useful only if we can identify which ones deserve further attention.

The ability to generate expert-sounding analysis is useful only if its claims can withstand scrutiny.

And the ability to automate work benefits society only if the resulting productivity creates better outcomes for people.

The future of work may be less about producing answers and more about establishing which answers are worth acting on.

That is where I expect much of the remaining human work—and much of the value—to move.
